sections.skill: Compare checking accounts and complete the steps to open one

questions.prompt: Jordan is 17 and wants a first checking account. Which plan matches how most banks handle an applicant under 18?

choices.text: Open an individual account online using only a student ID card
Wait until age 21, the legal minimum age for any bank account
Deposit paychecks into a friend's account until Jordan turns 18
Open a joint teen account with a parent or guardian

questions.correct_answer: Open a joint teen account with a parent or guardian
questions.intro: Banks and credit unions usually require an adult (18 or older) to open an account alone, because a minor generally cannot be held to a contract. Many offer teen or student checking accounts that a minor opens jointly with a parent or guardian. The adult co-owner can see the account and shares responsibility for it.
questions.feedback: Most institutions let a minor open a checking account only as a joint or teen account with an adult co-owner.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a school ID meets the identity requirements
misconceptions.B: Invents a minimum age for every account
misconceptions.C: Thinks sharing someone else's account is safe or allowed

questions.prompt: Which information will a bank most likely require to open a checking account?

choices.text: Your report card, a teacher's reference, and your school's address
Your credit card number and its PIN, to link the two accounts
Only a signature, because banks do not verify who customers are
Name, birth date, address, and an ID number such as an SSN

questions.correct_answer: Name, birth date, address, and an ID number such as an SSN
questions.intro: Federal rules require banks to verify who opens an account. Before opening one, a bank collects at least your name, date of birth, address, and an identification number: a Social Security number for U.S. citizens, or another number, such as an ITIN or passport number, for others. Most banks also ask for a government-issued photo ID.
questions.feedback: The Customer Identification Program rule requires name, date of birth, address, and an ID number; banks usually also check a photo ID.

misconceptions.B: Thinks sharing a PIN is part of opening an account

questions.prompt:
Tess will receive about $800 a month by direct deposit and usually keeps about $300 in checking.
Account X: $10 monthly fee, waived with a direct deposit of $500 or more each month.
Account Y: $5 monthly fee, waived if the balance stays at $1,000 or more.
What would each account cost Tess in monthly fees over a year?

choices.text: Account X: $0; Account Y: $60
Account X: $120; Account Y: $60
Account X: $0; Account Y: $0
Account X: $120; Account Y: $0

questions.intro: Many checking accounts charge a monthly maintenance fee that is waived if you meet a condition: a minimum balance, a minimum direct deposit, or being a student. Compare accounts by the fees YOU would actually pay, based on how you will use the account.
questions.feedback: Tess's $800 direct deposit meets Account X's $500 condition, so X costs $0. Her $300 balance is below Y's $1,000, so Y costs $5 × 12 = $60.

misconceptions.B: Ignores Account X's direct deposit waiver
misconceptions.C: Assumes Tess meets Account Y's $1,000 balance rule

questions.prompt: Tess wants her paycheck deposited directly into her new account. What does her employer need from her?

choices.text: Her debit card number and its PIN
Her online banking username and password
Only the name of her bank and the branch's street address
Her bank's routing number and her account number

questions.correct_answer: Her bank's routing number and her account number
questions.intro: Direct deposit sends pay electronically into your account. Your employer needs two numbers: the routing number, a 9-digit number that identifies your bank, and your account number, which identifies your account at that bank. Both appear on checks and in the bank's app. Never share a PIN or password to set up a deposit.
questions.feedback: Routing number plus account number tells the payroll system exactly where to send the money. PINs and passwords are never needed.

misconceptions.A: Confuses a debit card with the account itself; unsafe
misconceptions.B: Thinks an employer needs login credentials; unsafe
misconceptions.C: Thinks a bank name identifies a specific account

questions.prompt: Ahmed's new account requires a $25 opening deposit and has a $6 monthly fee that is waived only when the balance stays at $300 or more. Ahmed's balance stays below $300 (around $150) every month. Assuming no other fees, how much will the account charge him in fees over 6 months?
questions.feedback: The fee applies each of the 6 months because the balance never reaches $300: $6 × 6 = $36. The $25 opening deposit is Ahmed's own money in the account, not a fee.

misconceptions.B: Counts one month only
misconceptions.D: Adds the opening deposit as if it were a fee

sections.relationship: Choosing and opening an account depends on understanding what a monthly fee and a waiver condition are.

questions.prompt: A checking account has a "$12 monthly maintenance fee." What does this mean?

choices.text: The bank takes $12 each month unless a waiver applies
The bank pays you $12 each month for keeping the account
You must deposit $12 every month to keep the account open
You pay $12 one time, when you first open the account

questions.correct_answer: The bank takes $12 each month unless a waiver applies
questions.intro: A fee is a charge the bank takes from your account. A "monthly maintenance fee" (also called a service fee) is charged every month just for having the account, unless you meet a waiver condition.
questions.feedback: A monthly maintenance fee is taken from your account each month unless you qualify for a waiver.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a fee with interest
misconceptions.C: Confuses a fee with a deposit requirement
misconceptions.D: Thinks a monthly fee is charged once

questions.prompt: An account waives its $8 monthly fee "with a minimum daily balance of $500." In March, Lena's balance stays above $600 every day. What fee does she pay for March?
questions.intro: A waiver condition is a rule that, if you meet it, cancels a fee. A "minimum daily balance" rule means your balance must stay at or above the amount every day of the statement period.
questions.feedback: Lena's balance never dropped below $500, so the fee is waived: $0.

misconceptions.B: Halves the fee
misconceptions.D: Confuses the balance requirement with a fee

questions.prompt: An account waives its $8 monthly fee "with a minimum daily balance of $500." In April, Lena's balance drops to $450 for one day, then goes back above $600. What fee does she pay for April?
questions.intro: With a minimum daily balance rule, one day below the minimum is enough to lose the waiver for that month, even if the balance is high on other days.
questions.feedback: One day at $450 is below $500, so the $8 fee applies for April.

misconceptions.A: Uses the average or ending balance instead of the daily minimum
misconceptions.B: Prorates the fee

choices.text: It is your own money, deposited into your new account
It is a fee the bank keeps to open the account
It is a loan the bank gives you to start the account
It must be paid again every month you keep the account

questions.correct_answer: It is your own money, deposited into your new account
questions.feedback: An opening deposit is the first money you put into the account. It stays yours.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a deposit with a fee
misconceptions.C: Confuses a deposit with a loan

questions.prompt: Two accounts are identical except for fees. Which would cost a student nothing?

choices.text: One with a $3 fee, because the fee is small
One with a $15 fee waived at a $5,000 balance, for a student with $200
One with a fee charged only every other month, at $6
One whose fee is waived for students, if the student qualifies

questions.correct_answer: One whose fee is waived for students, if the student qualifies
questions.feedback: Only an account whose fee the student can actually avoid costs nothing.

misconceptions.A: Thinks a small fee is the same as no fee
misconceptions.B: Ignores whether the student can meet the waiver

sections.skill: Reading account disclosures and fee schedules

questions.prompt: A disclosure says: "Paper statement fee: $2 per month. Free with e-statements." Rafael wants paper statements. Over two years, how much will this choice cost?
questions.intro: When you open an account, the bank gives you disclosures: documents that list the account's interest rate, fees, and rules. Federal law (the Truth in Savings Act) requires banks to disclose this information. Small optional fees, like paper statement fees, are easy to miss.
questions.feedback: $2 per month × 24 months = $48.

misconceptions.B: Counts one charge per year

questions.prompt: Which item would you expect to find in an account's fee schedule?

choices.text: The charge for an incoming or outgoing wire transfer
The bank's current interest rate on 30-year home mortgages
The FDIC insurance limit for your account
The interest rate on your credit card

questions.correct_answer: The charge for an incoming or outgoing wire transfer
questions.intro: A fee schedule is a list of every fee the account can charge: monthly fees, overdraft and returned item fees, wire transfer fees, stop payment fees, out-of-network ATM fees, and fees for extras like paper statements or cashier's checks.
questions.feedback: Wire transfer fees are account fees listed in a fee schedule.

misconceptions.B: Confuses a fee schedule with a loan rate sheet
misconceptions.D: Confuses a deposit fee schedule with a card agreement

questions.prompt: An account advertises "No monthly fee!" Its fee schedule lists a $35 overdraft fee, a $3 out-of-network ATM fee, and a $30 wire fee. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: The account has no fees of any kind
The account will cost exactly $68 every month, since all three fees apply
Every one of those fees is illegal for a free account
The account can still be costly, depending on how it is used

questions.correct_answer: The account can still be costly, depending on how it is used
questions.feedback: "No monthly fee" covers only the maintenance fee. Other fees apply when you use certain services or overdraw.

misconceptions.A: Treats the ad as the whole story
misconceptions.B: Adds possible fees as if all are charged monthly
misconceptions.C: Thinks a free account cannot have any fees

questions.prompt: A bank sends a notice that a fee will change in 30 days. What is a reasonable response?

choices.text: Compare the new terms with other accounts
Ignore it, because fees cannot change after an account is opened
Close the account the same day without checking alternatives
Pay the new fee now to lock in the old rate

questions.correct_answer: Compare the new terms with other accounts
questions.intro: Banks can change account terms. They must tell existing customers in advance about changes that could hurt them, such as a higher fee. That notice gives you time to compare and decide.
questions.feedback: Advance notice lets you compare and, if needed, move your money before the change takes effect.

misconceptions.B: Thinks account terms are fixed forever
misconceptions.D: Invents a way to lock in fees

choices.text: Which bank has the larger headquarters building?
Which disclosure document is longer?
Which bank's advertising do I see most often on social media?

questions.correct_answer: Which fees will I realistically pay, given how I bank?

misconceptions.A: Uses size as a measure of cost
misconceptions.B: Uses document length as a measure of cost

questions.prompt: Devon's application for a checking account is denied because of a report from a checking account screening company. What kind of history does such a report usually show?

choices.text: Unpaid overdrafts or fraud at past banks
Grades and attendance from high school
Devon's medical history and doctor visits
Every purchase Devon has made with cash

questions.correct_answer: Unpaid overdrafts or fraud at past banks
questions.intro: Before opening an account, many banks check a consumer report from a checking account screening company, such as ChexSystems or Early Warning Services. These reports list problems with past accounts, such as unpaid overdrafts, accounts closed by a bank, or suspected fraud. Negative information can stay on these reports for years.
questions.feedback: Screening reports focus on past deposit-account problems, such as unpaid negative balances or fraud.

misconceptions.B: Thinks banks screen school records

questions.prompt: Devon was denied a checking account because of a checking account screening report that he believes contains a mistake. What can he do?

choices.text: Nothing, because screening reports cannot be corrected
Pay the screening company to delete it
Open new accounts under a friend's name instead of his own
Request a free copy of the report and dispute the error

questions.correct_answer: Request a free copy of the report and dispute the error
questions.intro: Checking account screening companies are consumer reporting agencies. Under federal law you can get a free copy of your report every 12 months and dispute information you believe is wrong; the company must investigate.
questions.feedback: Like credit reports, screening reports can be requested for free each year and disputed when wrong.

misconceptions.B: Thinks deletion can be bought

questions.prompt: Devon's checking account screening report correctly shows a $90 negative balance he left at an old bank. Which step would most likely help him open an account in the future?

choices.text: Pay off the $90 and ask the old bank to update the report
Wait one week, because reports clear automatically
Open many applications at once to find one bank that says yes
Avoid banks and keep all of his money in cash

questions.correct_answer: Pay off the $90 and ask the old bank to update the report
questions.feedback: Paying what is owed and having the record updated to "paid" improves his chances. Keeping cash at home adds theft and loss risks.

misconceptions.B: Thinks negative records vanish quickly
misconceptions.D: Gives up the protection of an insured account

questions.prompt: What is a "second-chance" checking account?

choices.text: A second account that the bank opens automatically for every customer
A loan that pays off your old bank's balance
A savings account that pays double interest
An account for people with past account problems, often with limits

questions.correct_answer: An account for people with past account problems, often with limits
questions.intro: Some banks and credit unions offer second-chance accounts to people who were denied regular accounts. They may have a monthly fee, no overdraft feature, or lower limits. After a period of good use, some can be changed to a regular account.
questions.feedback: Second-chance accounts help people rebuild banking history, often with limits or fees.

misconceptions.B: Confuses an account with a loan

questions.prompt: Devon cannot open a regular account, but a credit union offers him a second-chance checking account (an account for people with past account problems, often with a small fee). Why might it be better than using check-cashing stores for every paycheck?

choices.text: Check-cashing stores are always free
Second-chance accounts pay much higher interest than savings accounts
A bank account means Devon can never overdraw again
Check-cashing fees on every paycheck can cost far more over a year

questions.correct_answer: Check-cashing fees on every paycheck can cost far more over a year
questions.feedback: For example, 2% of a $900 paycheck every two weeks is $18 per check, about $468 a year, which is usually much more than an account's fees.

misconceptions.A: Assumes check cashing has no fees
misconceptions.B: Invents a high interest rate
misconceptions.C: Thinks an account prevents all overdrafts
